source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 1: Risk and Basic Risk Management Framework

facts.statement: Risks are uncertainties resulting in adverse outcomes, adverse in relation to planned objectives or expectations; financial risks are uncertainties resulting in adverse variation of profitability or outright losses. Uncertainty is imprecise knowledge about future events; risk is the kind of uncertainty that can be systematically assessed through a reasonably reliable probability distribution of outcomes and therefore measured and priced. Uncertainties in cash inflows and outflows create variations in net cash flow, which may be favourable or unfavourable; the possible unfavourable impact is the risk. Lower risk implies lower variability in net cash flow, with lower upside and downside potential; higher risk implies higher upside and downside potential; zero risk implies no variation in net cash flow, and its return is low compared with other opportunities.

The capital required by a business should be enough to meet the maximum loss that may arise so as to avoid bankruptcy, so a business with wider variation in net cash flow has higher risk, higher potential profit and loss, and a higher capital requirement. Expected returns relate to risk: when two investments give the same return but one has a steadier cash flow, the less risky one is preferred, and the extra return demanded for higher risk is the risk premium or cost of risk. Risk adjusted return nets risk against return; risk adjusted return on capital (RAROC) is the key driver for investment decisions and a better performance measure than return on assets or return on equity because those ignore the risk taken to get the returns. The higher the risk in a business model, the higher the capital requirement and the return expectation.

Risk needs to be managed because adverse variation in uncertain factors can be severe and wipe out capital and threaten survival; the loss potential must be limited to a level the organisation can absorb. Measuring risk lets an organisation know its potential losses in adverse situations and the capital needed. The probability of loss is factored into pricing: overestimating losses overprices and loses business, underestimating them lowers profits and the planned RAROC. Risk management involves identification, measurement, control, mitigation and estimating the costs of risk, and needs a separate setup and a well-defined framework.

The risk management framework has well-articulated processes covering organisation, risk identification, risk measurement, risk pricing, risk monitoring and control, and risk mitigation. Organisation: the Board of Directors has overall responsibility and sets policy and limits; the Risk Management Committee is a Board sub-committee that sets guidelines, ensures processes conform to policy, sets prudential limits and ensures robust measurement models; senior executive committees (ALCO, Credit Risk Management Committee, Operational Risk Management Committee) implement policy; a risk management department headed by a Chief Risk Officer, with groups for asset-liability, mid office, credit risk and operational risk, supports them. ALCO oversees liquidity risk, monitors net interest margin and recommends lending rates to the Board; the CRMC ensures robustness of credit risk, prepares rating distribution and migration charts and probability of default and clears new credit products; the ORMC ensures robustness of operational risk, analyses frauds and clears new non-credit products.

Risk identification examines the risks of a transaction and their effect on the portfolio and capital. The courseware example is a loan of ₹1 crore for five years at 1 per cent over the benchmark prime lending rate, funded by a three-year fixed rate deposit: funding risk (liquidity) arises when the deposit matures at the end of three years while the loan is still outstanding; time risk if the borrower defaults; basis risk when the lending rate floats and the deposit rate is fixed; gap or mismatch risk; reinvestment risk when loan repayments are redeployed at a different rate; embedded option risk from prepayment or premature withdrawal; plus default (credit) risk and operational risk.

Quantitative measures of risk are of three kinds: based on sensitivity (the change in a target variable for a unit move in one market parameter, for example duration or the interest rate gap; it considers only one parameter and depends on current conditions), based on volatility (the standard deviation of the values of a variable, the square root of the variance; historical volatility from past data, implied volatility from option prices) and based on downside potential (potential losses and their probabilities, which captures only adverse deviations; value at risk is a downside measure and the most comprehensive, relied on by banks and regulators). Volatility over a horizon T equals daily volatility times the square root of T. Risk measures are forward looking and estimate possible losses within a confidence level using historical data.

Risk pricing must take into account the cost of deployable funds, operating expenses, loss probabilities, the capital charge and the profit margin or return on net worth; the cost of funds must correspond to the term for which funds are deployed; pricing is transaction based. If past experience shows an average loss of 2 per cent on accounts of a given risk level, a risk premium of 2 per cent may be added.

Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed from 1 April 2016 are priced with reference to the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) as the internal benchmark; MCLR comprises marginal cost of funds, negative carry on account of CRR, operating costs and tenor premium; negative carry on CRR is calculated as required CRR times marginal cost divided by (1 minus CRR); a bank reviews and publishes MCLR of different maturities every month on a pre-announced date; the reset periodicity under MCLR is one year or lower. All floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto and so on) and floating rate loans extended by banks to MSMEs must be benchmarked to an External Benchmark Rate, with a uniform benchmark within a loan category; the rate under an external benchmark is reset at least once in three months; the bank is free to decide the spread, but the credit risk premium may change only when the borrower's credit assessment undergoes a substantial change as agreed in the loan contract, and other spread components including operating cost may be altered once in three years (reduced earlier for retention on justifiable grounds). Existing Base Rate and BPLR loans continue until repayment or renewal.

facts.statement: Risk monitoring needs an organisational structure, a comprehensive measurement approach, policies and guidelines, prudential and discretionary limits, a strong management information system, effective control and reporting procedures, a risk management framework independent of operational departments, periodical review and a robust audit system; senior management and the board receive regular reports and a Board Committee on Risk Management verifies the internal controls; reviews include large exposures, risk concentrations and stress testing. Risk mitigation eliminates or reduces uncertainty, and while it reduces downside variability it also reduces upside potential. Credit risk is mitigated by collateral, guarantees and credit derivatives; interest rate risk by swaps, forward rate agreements and futures; forex risk by forwards, options and futures. Exchanges act as central counterparty to reduce counterparty risk; the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd, set up in April 2001, is the central counterparty for government securities, USD-INR and forex forward segments.

Diversification reduces risk because variations in cash flows of different businesses are not all in the same direction; the risk of a portfolio is less than the weighted average of the risks of its parts. In the courseware example five businesses each had a ratio of standard deviation to mean between 36 per cent and 61 per cent while the combined portfolio had 25 per cent. Enterprise-wide risk management is a continuous, structured process of listing objectives, identifying external and internal risk factors, prioritising them, exploring mitigation and controlling and monitoring them across the whole organisation. The COSO enterprise risk management framework has eight components (internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring) and four objectives (strategic, operations, reporting, compliance); risk responses are avoidance, reduction, transfer and acceptance.

payload.title: Uncertainty, risk and the variation in cash flow
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Risk** = an **uncertainty with an adverse outcome**, measured against the **plan or expectation**. **Financial risk** = uncertainty that causes **adverse variation in profit or an outright loss**.

**Uncertainty vs risk**
- **Uncertainty**: **vague** knowledge of what may happen.
- **Risk**: uncertainty that can be given a **reasonably reliable probability distribution** of outcomes, so it can be **measured and priced**.

**Why it matters to cash flow**: uncertain **inflows** (sales volume and price) and **outflows** (purchase and running costs) make **net cash flow vary**. The **unfavourable part of that variation is the risk**.

| Variability of net cash flow | Upside and downside | Return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Low** | smaller | smaller |
| **High** | larger | larger |
| **None (zero risk)** | none | **low** compared with other opportunities |

payload.title: Risk, capital and return move together
payload.core_explanation_md:
- **Capital** must be enough to absorb the **maximum loss** so the business is not bankrupted. **More variation in net cash flow = more risk = more possible profit and loss = more capital.**
- **Return** must pay for the risk. Between two investments with the **same total return**, the one with the **steadier** flow is preferred; the **extra return** asked for **higher risk** is the **risk premium (cost of risk)**.
- **Risk adjusted return on capital (RAROC)**: return **netted against risk** relative to the capital employed. It is better than **ROA or ROE** because those **ignore the risk taken to earn the return**, so they cannot fairly compare business lines with different risk.

**The linkage**: **the higher the risk in a business model, the higher the capital needed and the higher the return expected.**

payload.title: Why a bank must manage risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
- Adverse swings can be **severe and wipe out capital**, so **survival** is at stake. The **loss potential** must be kept at a level the bank can **absorb**.
- **Measuring** risk tells the bank **how much it could lose** in bad conditions and **how much capital** that needs.
- The **probability of loss is built into price**: **overestimating** it **overprices and loses business**; **underestimating** it **cuts profit and the planned RAROC**.
- Risk management = **identify, measure, control, mitigate** and **estimate the cost** of risk. It needs **specialist skills** and a **separate set-up** with a **defined framework**.

payload.title: The risk management organisation and the six processes
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Six processes**: **organisation**, **risk identification**, **measurement**, **pricing**, **monitoring and control**, **mitigation**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Board of Directors** | **overall responsibility**; sets **policy** and **limits** |
| **Risk Management Committee** (Board sub-committee) | guidelines, **conformity to policy**, **prudential limits**, **robust models**, adequate staffing |
| **ALCO** | **liquidity risk**, **net interest margin**, **recommends lending rates** to the Board, mid office monitoring of treasury |
| **Credit Risk Management Committee** | **rating processes**, **rating distribution and migration charts**, **probability of default**, portfolio analysis, **clears new credit products** |
| **Operational Risk Management Committee** | **operational risk robustness**, **fraud analysis**, **clears new non-credit products** |
| **Risk management department** | headed by the **Chief Risk Officer**; groups for **asset-liability (market risk)**, **mid office**, **credit** and **operational** risk; **independent monitoring and reporting** |

payload.title: Spotting the risks in one loan
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank lends **₹1 crore for 5 years** at **BPLR + 1%**, funded by a **3-year fixed deposit**:

| Risk | Why it arises |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding (liquidity) risk** | the **deposit falls due after 3 years** while the **loan runs 5** |
| **Time risk** | if the borrower **defaults**, repayment is **late** |
| **Basis risk** | the **loan rate floats** but the **deposit rate is fixed** |
| **Gap / mismatch risk** | **repricing and maturity mismatch** between assets and liabilities |
| **Reinvestment risk** | **repayments** must be **redeployed at a different rate** |
| **Embedded option risk** | **prepayment** of the loan or **early withdrawal** of the deposit |
| **Default (credit) risk** and **operational risk** | the borrower fails; processes fail |

Risk is **taken at the transaction level**, but **capital is set at the portfolio level**; some risks (liquidity, interest rate) are **managed in aggregate**.

payload.title: Measuring risk: sensitivity, volatility and downside potential
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Measure | What it shows | Examples and limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sensitivity** | change in a **target variable** for a **unit move in one market parameter** | **duration**, **interest rate gap**; looks at **one parameter only**, depends on **current conditions** |
| **Volatility** | **standard deviation** of a variable (**square root of variance**) | **historical** (from past data) or **implied** (from option prices, forward looking) |
| **Downside potential** | **possible losses and their probabilities** (only the **adverse** side) | **Value at Risk (VaR)**; **most comprehensive**; used by banks and regulators |

**Square root of time rule**: **volatility over T periods = volatility per period × √T**.

All the measures are **forward-looking estimates**, built on **historical data**, at a stated **confidence level**.

payload.title: Pricing a loan for its risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
A transaction must be priced to cover **five things**:

1. **Cost of deployable funds** (matched to the **term** for which they are deployed).
2. **Operating expenses**.
3. **Loss probability** (expected loss).
4. **Capital charge** (the cost of the capital the loan needs).
5. **Profit margin or return on net worth**.

If **history shows 2% average loss** on accounts of a given risk level, **add a 2% risk premium** to the price. Pricing is **transaction based**, which is why risk is **measured at transaction level**.

payload.title: Lending rates: MCLR and external benchmarks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**MCLR (internal benchmark)**: floating rupee loans **sanctioned or renewed from 1 April 2016**.
- **Components**: **marginal cost of funds**, **negative carry on CRR**, **operating costs**, **tenor premium**.
- **Negative carry on CRR** = **required CRR × marginal cost ÷ (1 − CRR)**.
- **Reviewed and published monthly** (each maturity) on a pre-announced date; **reset periodicity one year or lower**.

**External benchmark**: **all floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.) and floating rate loans to MSMEs** must be linked to an **External Benchmark Rate**; **one benchmark per loan category**; **reset at least once in three months**.

**Spread under an external benchmark**: the bank sets it, but **credit risk premium changes only on a substantial change in credit assessment** (as agreed in the contract); **other components, including operating cost, only once in three years** (can be cut earlier to retain customers).

**Old loans**: **Base Rate and BPLR loans continue** to repayment or renewal.

payload.title: Monitoring, mitigating and the central counterparty
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Monitoring and control** needs: a **structure**, a **measurement approach**, **policies and limits**, a strong **MIS**, **independent risk management** apart from operating departments, **periodic review**, and **audit**. Management and the Board get **regular risk reports**; a **Board Committee on Risk Management** checks the controls; reviews cover **large exposures, concentrations and stress tests**.

**Mitigation** lowers **downside variability**, but also **cuts upside**.
- **Credit risk**: **collateral**, **guarantees**, **credit derivatives**.
- **Interest rate risk**: **swaps**, **forward rate agreements**, **futures**.
- **Forex risk**: **forwards**, **options**, **futures**.

**Counterparty risk** falls when an **exchange or central counterparty** stands in the middle. **CCIL** (set up **April 2001**) is the **central counterparty** for **government securities, USD-INR and forex forward** segments.

payload.title: Diversification and enterprise-wide risk management
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification**: business cash flows do not all move together, so **portfolio risk is less than the weighted average of the parts' risks**. (The courseware: five businesses with a **ratio of standard deviation to mean of 36% to 61%**, but **25% for the combined portfolio**.)

**EWRM**: a **continuous, structured process** to **list objectives, identify internal and external risk factors, prioritise them, explore mitigation, and control and monitor** them, across **the whole organisation**.

**COSO ERM framework**
- **Eight components**: **internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring**.
- **Four objectives**: **strategic, operations, reporting, compliance**.
- **Risk responses**: **avoid, reduce, transfer, accept**.

payload.title: Turning a daily volatility into a longer one
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bond fund has a daily volatility of 0.8%. What is its volatility over 25 days, using the square root of time rule, and what daily volatility would give 9% over 36 days?
payload.final_answer_with_unit: 4% over 25 days; a daily volatility of 1.5% gives 9% over 36 days

self_check.prompt_text: Why does volatility grow with the square root of time and not in proportion to time?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Daily random moves partly offset one another, so the spread of outcomes grows more slowly than the number of days.

payload.title: Diversification: two businesses whose cash flows offset
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: over eight years Business P earns (in ₹ lakh) 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 and Business Q earns 8, 6, 6, 6, 5, 5, 3, 1. Compare the variability of each with that of the two together, using standard deviation (population) and the ratio to the mean.

worked_steps.description: Standard deviation of P (and of Q, by the same sum).
Ratio of standard deviation to mean for each.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Each business has a standard deviation of 2 (40% of its mean), but together they give a steady 10 a year with no variation

self_check.prompt_text: Would the combined risk fall this much if both businesses moved in the same direction?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The fall comes from their opposite movements; the more similar the movements, the smaller the benefit.

payload.title: Negative carry on CRR in the MCLR
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has a marginal cost of funds of 6.50% and the required CRR is 4%. Find the negative carry on CRR that goes into the MCLR.

worked_steps.description: Express as a rate, rounded to four places.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The negative carry on CRR is 0.2708% a year

self_check.prompt_text: Why is there a negative carry on CRR at all?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank pays no return on CRR balances, so the cost of funds held there is a loss that must be recovered in the lending rate.

payload.stem_md: Which statement best separates risk from uncertainty?

options.text_md: Risk is certain; uncertainty is not
Risk is uncertainty that can be assessed through a reasonably reliable probability distribution of outcomes

options.explanation_md: Only risk can be measured and priced.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Uncertainty is imprecise knowledge; risk is the kind that can be systematically assessed, measured and priced.

payload.stem_md: A trader's purchase price rises unexpectedly while his sale price is fixed. What happens to net cash flow?

options.text_md: It varies adversely, which is the risk element at work
options.explanation_md: Higher costs reduce net cash flow.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Uncertainty in cash outflows creates variation in net cash flow; the unfavourable variation is the risk.

payload.stem_md: What does a zero-risk investment imply?

options.text_md: No variation in net cash flow, with a low return compared with other opportunities

payload.correct_explanation_md: Zero risk implies no variation in net cash flow and a return that is low compared with other opportunities.

payload.stem_md: Two investments give the same total return over five years, but the first has a steady cash flow and the second a widely varying one. How does the courseware reason?

options.text_md: The first is preferred; the second would need a higher return as a risk premium
The second is preferred as it can earn more

payload.correct_explanation_md: A steadier cash flow is preferred; extra return demanded for higher risk is the risk premium or cost of risk.

payload.stem_md: Why is RAROC a better performance measure than return on equity?

options.text_md: Because it takes into account the risk undertaken to get the returns

payload.correct_explanation_md: ROA and ROE ignore the risk taken to get the returns; RAROC factors it in.

payload.stem_md: A bank overestimates the loss on a class of loans and prices them accordingly. What is the likely result?

options.explanation_md: This is the stated risk of overestimation.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Overestimation of loss results in overpricing and loss of business; underestimation lowers profits.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT listed as part of controlling risk to the organisation's capacity to bear it?

options.text_md: Mitigation and estimating the costs of risk
Maximising the upside potential of every exposure

payload.correct_explanation_md: Risk management requires identification, measurement, control, mitigation and estimating the costs of risk.

payload.stem_md: Which body oversees the liquidity risk of the bank, monitors its net interest margin and recommends lending rates to the Board?
payload.correct_explanation_md: ALCO oversees liquidity risk, monitors net interest margin and recommends lending rates to the Board.

payload.stem_md: Which committee clears new credit products and prepares rating migration charts and probabilities of default?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The CRMC ensures the robustness of credit risk, prepares rating distribution and migration charts and probability of default, and clears new credit products.

payload.stem_md: A bank funds a five-year floating rate loan with a three-year fixed deposit. Which risk arises because the deposit rate is fixed while the loan rate floats?

options.explanation_md: Arises from prepayment or early withdrawal.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Basis risk arises when the loan rate is linked to a floating benchmark while the deposit carries a fixed rate.

payload.stem_md: What is reinvestment risk in the courseware's loan example?

options.text_md: The loan repayments have to be redeployed at a rate that may differ from the rate on the loan

payload.correct_explanation_md: As the loan is repaid, the proceeds must be deployed elsewhere at a rate that may differ, giving reinvestment risk.

payload.stem_md: Which measure captures the change in a target variable for a unit move in a single market parameter?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Sensitivity measures the deviation of a target variable due to a unit movement of a single market parameter.

payload.stem_md: Volatility is:

options.text_md: The standard deviation, being the square root of the variance

payload.correct_explanation_md: Volatility is the standard deviation, the square root of the variance of the random variable.

payload.stem_md: Which is the most comprehensive measure of risk, integrating sensitivity and volatility with the adverse effect of uncertainty?

options.text_md: Downside potential, of which value at risk is an example

payload.correct_explanation_md: Downside potential is the most comprehensive measure; value at risk is a downside risk measure.

payload.stem_md: Implied volatility differs from historical volatility in that it is:

options.text_md: Computed from option prices and forward looking

payload.correct_explanation_md: Implied volatility is derived from option prices and reflects the market's view of future moves; historical volatility measures past changes.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT one of the five factors the courseware says pricing must take into account?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Pricing takes into account cost of funds, operating expenses, loss probabilities, capital charge and profit margin.

payload.stem_md: Past experience shows an average loss of 2 per cent on accounts of a given risk level. How is this reflected in pricing?

options.text_md: A risk premium of 2 per cent is added
options.explanation_md: The expected loss is priced in.

options.text_md: The rate is cut by 2 per cent

payload.correct_explanation_md: The historical loss is the cost of the risk and may be factored into pricing as a risk premium.

payload.stem_md: From which date are floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed priced with reference to MCLR as the internal benchmark?

options.explanation_md: That is when the Base Rate began.
That is the external benchmark date in the courseware.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned and renewed from 1 April 2016 are priced with reference to MCLR.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a component of MCLR under the Directions?

options.text_md: Negative carry on account of CRR
Credit risk premium of the borrower
options.explanation_md: This belongs to the spread, not MCLR.

payload.correct_explanation_md: MCLR comprises marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating costs and tenor premium; credit risk premium is part of the spread.

payload.stem_md: How often must the interest rate under an external benchmark linked loan be reset at the least?

options.text_md: At least once in three months

options.explanation_md: That is the outer limit for MCLR.
That is for other spread components.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The interest rate under an external benchmark is reset at least once in three months.

payload.stem_md: Under an external benchmark system, when may a bank change the credit risk premium of an existing borrower?

options.text_md: Only when the borrower's credit assessment undergoes a substantial change, as agreed in the loan contract
Only once in three years regardless of credit
options.explanation_md: The three-year rule is for other components.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The credit risk premium may undergo change only when the borrower's credit assessment undergoes a substantial change, as agreed in the loan contract.

payload.stem_md: Which loans must be linked to an external benchmark?

options.text_md: Floating rate personal or retail loans such as housing and auto, and floating rate loans to MSMEs

payload.correct_explanation_md: All floating rate personal or retail loans and floating rate loans to MSMEs must be benchmarked to an External Benchmark Rate.

payload.stem_md: Which agency acts as central counterparty for government securities, USD-INR and forex forward segments, per the courseware?

options.text_md: The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd

payload.correct_explanation_md: CCIL, set up in April 2001, acts as a central counterparty in those segments.

payload.stem_md: What is the trade-off in risk mitigation?

options.text_md: It reduces downside variability but also reduces upside potential

payload.correct_explanation_md: Risk mitigation reduces downside variability and the upside potential simultaneously.

payload.stem_md: Why is portfolio risk less than the weighted average of the risks of its parts?

options.text_md: Because risk is always zero in a portfolio
Because cash flow variations of the parts do not all move in the same direction

payload.correct_explanation_md: Variations in cash flows of different businesses are not unidirectional, so portfolio risk is lower.

payload.stem_md: How many components does the COSO enterprise risk management framework have, as described?

options.explanation_md: That is the number of objectives.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The COSO ERM framework has eight components and four objectives (strategic, operations, reporting, compliance).

payload.stem_md: A stock has a daily volatility of 1.2%. Using the square root of time rule, what is its volatility over 25 days, in per cent?
payload.correct_explanation_md: √25 = 5, so volatility = 1.2% × 5 = 6%.

payload.stem_md: A bank's marginal cost of funds is 7.2% and the required CRR is 4.5%. What is the negative carry on CRR in the MCLR, in per cent to four decimal places?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 4 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Negative carry = CRR × marginal cost ÷ (1 − CRR) = 4.5% × 7.2% ÷ (1 − 0.045) = 0.324 ÷ 0.955 = 0.33927, which rounds to 0.3393%.

payload.stem_md: A bank prices a loan with: cost of funds 6.80%, operating expenses 1.25%, loss probability 0.90%, capital charge 0.75% and profit margin 1.30%. What is the minimum loan rate, in per cent?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

unresolved: Most of this unit is the courseware's general account of risk; apart from the lending rate rules (checked against the Reserve Bank's Interest Rates on Advances Directions, 2025) no external source was read. The Directions are the 28 November 2025 text; later amendments were not compared.
RAROC is taught as the courseware describes it (a concept); no formula is stated because the courseware gives none.

The courseware's dates and descriptions for the BPLR (2003), Base Rate (1 July 2010) and the introduction of external benchmarks (1 April 2020) are not taught as exam points; the current Directions govern.
CCIL's date of establishment and role are the courseware's statements and were not verified against CCIL.

The courseware's volatility table (26 weekly prices) and its portfolio table are not reproduced; all figures here are new. The courseware uses a sample standard deviation in the portfolio table and a population one in the volatility table; the items here state which is used.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

items.title: Why a bank must manage risk
items.core_explanation_md:
- Adverse swings can be **severe and wipe out capital**, so **survival** is at stake. The **loss potential** must be kept at a level the bank can **absorb**.
- **Measuring** risk tells the bank **how much it could lose** in bad conditions and **how much capital** that needs.
- The **probability of loss is built into price**: **overestimating** it **overprices and loses business**; **underestimating** it **cuts profit and the planned RAROC**.
- Risk management = **identify, measure, control, mitigate** and **estimate the cost** of risk. It needs **specialist skills** and a **separate set-up** with a **defined framework**.

items.title: The risk management organisation and the six processes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Six processes**: **organisation**, **risk identification**, **measurement**, **pricing**, **monitoring and control**, **mitigation**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Board of Directors** | **overall responsibility**; sets **policy** and **limits** |
| **Risk Management Committee** (Board sub-committee) | guidelines, **conformity to policy**, **prudential limits**, **robust models**, adequate staffing |
| **ALCO** | **liquidity risk**, **net interest margin**, **recommends lending rates** to the Board, mid office monitoring of treasury |
| **Credit Risk Management Committee** | **rating processes**, **rating distribution and migration charts**, **probability of default**, portfolio analysis, **clears new credit products** |
| **Operational Risk Management Committee** | **operational risk robustness**, **fraud analysis**, **clears new non-credit products** |
| **Risk management department** | headed by the **Chief Risk Officer**; groups for **asset-liability (market risk)**, **mid office**, **credit** and **operational** risk; **independent monitoring and reporting** |

items.title: Spotting the risks in one loan
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank lends **₹1 crore for 5 years** at **BPLR + 1%**, funded by a **3-year fixed deposit**:

| Risk | Why it arises |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding (liquidity) risk** | the **deposit falls due after 3 years** while the **loan runs 5** |
| **Time risk** | if the borrower **defaults**, repayment is **late** |
| **Basis risk** | the **loan rate floats** but the **deposit rate is fixed** |
| **Gap / mismatch risk** | **repricing and maturity mismatch** between assets and liabilities |
| **Reinvestment risk** | **repayments** must be **redeployed at a different rate** |
| **Embedded option risk** | **prepayment** of the loan or **early withdrawal** of the deposit |
| **Default (credit) risk** and **operational risk** | the borrower fails; processes fail |

Risk is **taken at the transaction level**, but **capital is set at the portfolio level**; some risks (liquidity, interest rate) are **managed in aggregate**.

items.title: Measuring risk: sensitivity, volatility and downside potential
items.core_explanation_md:
| Measure | What it shows | Examples and limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sensitivity** | change in a **target variable** for a **unit move in one market parameter** | **duration**, **interest rate gap**; looks at **one parameter only**, depends on **current conditions** |
| **Volatility** | **standard deviation** of a variable (**square root of variance**) | **historical** (from past data) or **implied** (from option prices, forward looking) |
| **Downside potential** | **possible losses and their probabilities** (only the **adverse** side) | **Value at Risk (VaR)**; **most comprehensive**; used by banks and regulators |

**Square root of time rule**: **volatility over T periods = volatility per period × √T**.

All the measures are **forward-looking estimates**, built on **historical data**, at a stated **confidence level**.

items.title: Pricing a loan for its risk
items.core_explanation_md:
A transaction must be priced to cover **five things**:

1. **Cost of deployable funds** (matched to the **term** for which they are deployed).
2. **Operating expenses**.
3. **Loss probability** (expected loss).
4. **Capital charge** (the cost of the capital the loan needs).
5. **Profit margin or return on net worth**.

If **history shows 2% average loss** on accounts of a given risk level, **add a 2% risk premium** to the price. Pricing is **transaction based**, which is why risk is **measured at transaction level**.

items.title: Lending rates: MCLR and external benchmarks
items.core_explanation_md:
**MCLR (internal benchmark)**: floating rupee loans **sanctioned or renewed from 1 April 2016**.
- **Components**: **marginal cost of funds**, **negative carry on CRR**, **operating costs**, **tenor premium**.
- **Negative carry on CRR** = **required CRR × marginal cost ÷ (1 − CRR)**.
- **Reviewed and published monthly** (each maturity) on a pre-announced date; **reset periodicity one year or lower**.

**External benchmark**: **all floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.) and floating rate loans to MSMEs** must be linked to an **External Benchmark Rate**; **one benchmark per loan category**; **reset at least once in three months**.

**Spread under an external benchmark**: the bank sets it, but **credit risk premium changes only on a substantial change in credit assessment** (as agreed in the contract); **other components, including operating cost, only once in three years** (can be cut earlier to retain customers).

**Old loans**: **Base Rate and BPLR loans continue** to repayment or renewal.

items.title: Monitoring, mitigating and the central counterparty
items.core_explanation_md:
**Monitoring and control** needs: a **structure**, a **measurement approach**, **policies and limits**, a strong **MIS**, **independent risk management** apart from operating departments, **periodic review**, and **audit**. Management and the Board get **regular risk reports**; a **Board Committee on Risk Management** checks the controls; reviews cover **large exposures, concentrations and stress tests**.

**Mitigation** lowers **downside variability**, but also **cuts upside**.
- **Credit risk**: **collateral**, **guarantees**, **credit derivatives**.
- **Interest rate risk**: **swaps**, **forward rate agreements**, **futures**.
- **Forex risk**: **forwards**, **options**, **futures**.

**Counterparty risk** falls when an **exchange or central counterparty** stands in the middle. **CCIL** (set up **April 2001**) is the **central counterparty** for **government securities, USD-INR and forex forward** segments.

items.title: Diversification and enterprise-wide risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification**: business cash flows do not all move together, so **portfolio risk is less than the weighted average of the parts' risks**. (The courseware: five businesses with a **ratio of standard deviation to mean of 36% to 61%**, but **25% for the combined portfolio**.)

**EWRM**: a **continuous, structured process** to **list objectives, identify internal and external risk factors, prioritise them, explore mitigation, and control and monitor** them, across **the whole organisation**.

**COSO ERM framework**
- **Eight components**: **internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring**.
- **Four objectives**: **strategic, operations, reporting, compliance**.
- **Risk responses**: **avoid, reduce, transfer, accept**.

items.title: Turning a daily volatility into a longer one
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bond fund has a daily volatility of 0.8%. What is its volatility over 25 days, using the square root of time rule, and what daily volatility would give 9% over 36 days?
items.final_answer_with_unit: 4% over 25 days; a daily volatility of 1.5% gives 9% over 36 days

self_check.prompt_text: Why does volatility grow with the square root of time and not in proportion to time?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Daily random moves partly offset one another, so the spread of outcomes grows more slowly than the number of days.

items.title: Diversification: two businesses whose cash flows offset
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: over eight years Business P earns (in ₹ lakh) 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 and Business Q earns 8, 6, 6, 6, 5, 5, 3, 1. Compare the variability of each with that of the two together, using standard deviation (population) and the ratio to the mean.

worked_steps.description: Standard deviation of P (and of Q, by the same sum).
Ratio of standard deviation to mean for each.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Each business has a standard deviation of 2 (40% of its mean), but together they give a steady 10 a year with no variation

self_check.prompt_text: Would the combined risk fall this much if both businesses moved in the same direction?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The fall comes from their opposite movements; the more similar the movements, the smaller the benefit.
